prompt: A page runs 300 sequential database queries, each a 1 ms round trip within the data center. Roughly how long does the page take?
why: 300 × 1 ms = 300 ms of round trips alone. Batch into one query.
trap: Each query is "fast", but round trips add up.

prompt: Your app in Virginia makes 6 sequential calls to a service in Singapore for every page view.
why: A cross-Pacific round trip is ~200 ms, so 6 sequential calls is over a second. Colocate or batch.
trap: No amount of server tuning beats the speed of light.

prompt: Would keeping a 10 GB lookup table in RAM instead of reading it from SSD on each request make a meaningful difference?
tells: in RAM instead of reading it from SSD
why: RAM access is ~100 ns, an SSD read ~100 µs: about 1,000× apart.
trap: Both feel fast to a human; per request at scale, three orders of magnitude matter.

prompt: Can a single server sort 1 TB of data in under a minute? Estimate before building anything.
why: Even reading 1 TB from an SSD at ~2 GB/s takes ~8 minutes. Not on one machine.
trap: Parallelism might fix it, but the first move is the back-of-the-envelope check.

prompt: Would moving a hot config lookup from a Redis call in the same data center to an in-memory map make a difference at 50,000 lookups per second?
tells: Redis call in the same data center
why: ~0.5 ms network round trip vs ~100 ns memory: 50,000 × 0.5 ms = 25 seconds of waiting per second saved.
trap: Network round trips are thousands of times slower than memory.

prompt: A mobile app makes 15 sequential API calls on launch over a cellular connection with 80 ms round trips.
why: 15 × 80 ms = 1.2 s of pure waiting; batch or parallelize the calls.
trap: Knowing the round-trip cost tells you it's the count, not the payload, that hurts.

prompt: A job does 1 million random reads on a spinning hard disk. Will it finish in under a minute?
why: A seek is ~10 ms, so 1 million × 10 ms ≈ 2.8 hours. No.
trap: Sequential reads on the same disk would be fast; random access is the problem.

prompt: A trading firm wants a 5 ms round trip between New York and London.
why: ~5,600 km each way; light in fiber does ~200 km/ms, so ~56 ms round trip minimum. Physics says no.
trap: No amount of tuning beats the speed of light.
